questions.prompt: A gradient step subtracts a fixed multiple of the full gradient, so every coordinate moves together. Coordinate descent instead
options: minimizes in one coordinate while the others stay fixed
moves every coordinate by the same fixed length
replaces the objective by a random subset of its terms and keeps every coordinate free
requires the gradient to be zero before the first update
questions.explanation: One coordinate is free and the rest are data for that scalar problem. A common fixed length is a gradient step, not an exact coordinate minimization. A random subset of terms, with every coordinate still free, is a stochastic or incremental gradient step. The gradient need not vanish before the first update; the update is how a descent method searches.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x-6)^2+(y-1)^2+4(\lvert x\rvert+\lvert y\rvert)\) by one pass of exact coordinate minimization. The objective separates. What is the resulting \(x\)?
questions.explanation: The penalty weight is 4, so each coordinate is soft-thresholded at 2. The \(x\) center 6 is larger than 2, so \(x=6-2=4\). The \(y\) center 1 lies inside \([-2,2]\), so \(y\) becomes 0. Because the coordinates do not appear together, the order of the two updates does not change these values, and a second pass stays put. Reporting 6 leaves \(x\) unshrunk. Reporting 0 returns the \(y\) result.

questions.prompt: The objective \((x-2)^2+(y+3)^2+5(\lvert x\rvert+\lvert y\rvert)\) separates across coordinates. One pass of exact coordinate minimization
options: cannot move both coordinates, because a pass is allowed to touch only one of them
reaches the minimizer, and a second pass does not move either coordinate
reaches the minimizer only when the two updates are done in one prescribed order
stops at the first coordinate whose subdifferential contains 0, and leaves the other unchanged
questions.explanation: Each scalar problem ignores the other coordinate. Updating each one exactly, once, sets both to their soft-threshold values. Either order produces the same pair, so a prescribed order is not required for correctness. A pass through a separable problem is not limited to a single coordinate. A second pass sees the same scalar problems and stays put.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order of one exact coordinate update for \((x+y-2)^2+(x-4)^2\), updating \(x\) while \(y\) is frozen. Each step uses the value the previous step fixed.
questions.explanation: The frozen value has to be chosen before it can be substituted. The scalar function has to exist before it is minimized. The minimizer has to be known before \(x\) is replaced by it. Swapping an adjacent pair minimizes or substitutes a quantity that has not been fixed. The later update of \(y\) is a new pass step and is not one of these four.
steps: Freeze y at its current value and leave x free.
Write the objective as a function of x alone, with that frozen y inside (x+y-2).
Replace x by the minimizer just obtained.

questions.prompt: Start at \((0,0)\) and minimize \((x+y)^2+(x-4)^2\) by exact coordinate descent, updating \(x\) first and then \(y\). What is \(y\) after that one pass?
questions.explanation: With \(y\) frozen at 0 the objective in \(x\) is \(x^2+(x-4)^2\), whose derivative \(4x-8\) vanishes at \(x=2\). With \(x\) then frozen at 2 the objective in \(y\) is \((2+y)^2\), whose minimizer is \(y=-2\). The partial derivative in \(x\) at \((2,-2)\) equals \(-4\), not 0, so the pass has not reached a stationary point. Reporting 2 returns the updated \(x\). Reporting 0 leaves the start.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x-1)^2+(y-8)^2+6(\lvert x\rvert+\lvert y\rvert)\) by one exact coordinate pass. The objective separates. What is the resulting \(y\)?
questions.explanation: The threshold is \(6/2=3\). The center 8 is larger than 3, so \(y=8-3=5\). The center 1 lies inside \([-3,3]\), so \(x\) becomes 0. Reporting 8 leaves \(y\) unshrunk. Reporting 3 returns the threshold. Reporting 1 returns the \(x\) center.

questions.prompt: One coordinate has the scalar objective \(a(t-c)^2+\lambda\lvert t\rvert\) with \(a>0\) and \(c>\lambda/(2a)\). Write the minimizer in \(a\), \(c\), and \(\lambda\). Use the name lam for \(\lambda\).
questions.explanation:
At a positive minimizer the stationarity condition is \(2a(t-c)+\mathrm{lam}=0\). Solve for \(t\). The declared ranges keep \(c>\mathrm{lam}/(2a)\), so the positive branch is consistent.
• \(c-\mathrm{lam}/2\) drops the curvature \(a\).
• \(c-\mathrm{lam}/a\) drops the 2 from the square.
• \(c+\mathrm{lam}/(2a)\) moves away from zero.

questions.prompt: Along one coordinate, a gradient step of fixed length \(t\) subtracts \(t\) times the partial derivative. An exact coordinate update instead
options: uses that same fixed \(t\) on every coordinate and never solves a one-dimensional minimizer
chooses the coordinate value that minimizes the scalar function, which agrees with a gradient step only for a special length
requires the partial derivative to be undefined
moves a different coordinate from the one that was selected
questions.explanation: Exact minimization picks the best value of the free coordinate. For a smooth square, that value equals a gradient step only when the length is the exact line-search length \(1\) over the second derivative. A fixed length chosen in advance is not that update. The partial derivative is used when it exists, and the selected coordinate is the one that moves.

questions.prompt: Which objectives are minimized by one pass of exact coordinate updates, from any start?
options: \((x-1)^2+(y+2)^2+3(\lvert x\rvert+\lvert y\rvert)\)
\(\lvert x\rvert+(y-3)^2\)
questions.explanation: The first objective separates into a function of \(x\) plus a function of \(y\), and so does the third. One exact minimization of each coordinate finishes the problem. The second objective couples \(x\) and \(y\). From \((0,0)\), updating \(x\) then \(y\) lands at \((2,-2)\), where the partial derivative in \(x\) is \(-4\), not 0. The fourth couples the variables as well. From \((0,0)\), updating \(x\) then \(y\) lands at \((2,\ 0.5)\), where the partial derivative in \(x\) is 1, not 0.

questions.prompt: One step below is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails. The start is \((0,0)\), the objective is \((x+y)^2+(x-4)^2\), and the pass updates \(x\) and then \(y\).
questions.explanation: The two coordinate minimizations are right: \(x=2\) and then \(y=-2\). The partial derivative in \(x\) is \(2(x+y)+2(x-4)\). At \((2,-2)\) it equals \(-4\), not 0. The point is therefore not stationary, and another pass can still move \(x\). The false step claims that partial derivative vanishes.
steps: Freezing \(y\) at 0 and minimizing in \(x\) produces \(x=2\).
Freezing \(x\) at 2 and minimizing in \(y\) produces \(y=-2\).
At \((2,-2)\) the partial derivative with respect to \(x\) equals 0, so the point is stationary.
A later pass is still required when a partial derivative at the new point is nonzero.
reasons: The partial derivative in x at (2, -2) equals -4, not 0.
Freezing y at 0 does not produce x=2.
The partial derivative in y is the one that equals -4 at this point.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x+2)^2+(y-7)^2+2(\lvert x\rvert+\lvert y\rvert)\) by one exact coordinate pass. The objective separates. What is the resulting \(x\)?
questions.explanation: The threshold is \(2/2=1\). The center \(-2\) satisfies \(-2<-1\), so \(x=-2+1=-1\). The center 7 becomes \(7-1=6\). Reporting \(-2\) leaves \(x\) unshrunk. Reporting 6 returns \(y\). Reporting 1 returns the threshold.

questions.prompt: Each exact coordinate update of \((t-z)^2+\lambda\lvert t\rvert\) is the soft-threshold map at level \(\lambda/2\). That identity is the stationarity condition of the absolute penalty. Coordinate descent uses it when
options: the columns are orthonormal only, and otherwise the scalar problem has no minimizer
other coordinates are frozen, including inside a residual that still depends on them
the absolute value is replaced by a square before the update
every coordinate is updated by the same gradient entry
questions.explanation: Freezing the other coordinates leaves a scalar problem whose data term may still contain those frozen values. The minimizer of that scalar absolute-penalty problem is a soft threshold of the resulting center, whether or not a design matrix has orthonormal columns. Replacing the absolute value by a square is a different penalty. A shared gradient entry is a gradient step, not this exact update.
